lesson.title: Written in the Code: Molecular Evidence for Evolution
lesson.summary: Comparing DNA and protein sequences across species gives a direct, quantifiable measure of evolutionary relatedness, and the patterns it reveals independently confirm the family trees built from anatomy, embryology, and the fossil record.
lesson.body:
Every line of evidence covered so far in this unit, fossils, comparative anatomy, comparative embryology, biogeography, comes from observing organisms' bodies or their geographic distribution. Molecular evidence looks somewhere else entirely: the DNA sequence itself, the actual hereditary code passed down from parent to offspring, recalling the structure of that code from the DNA double helix. Because DNA is the molecule that is literally inherited, comparing it directly across species gives one of the most direct and quantifiable tests of evolutionary relationship available.

The starting point is something even more fundamental than any specific gene: essentially all known life uses the same genetic code, the same rules mapping sequences of DNA bases to sequences of amino acids in proteins, and the same basic molecular machinery for reading that code and building proteins from it. There is no chemical or physical requirement that life work this way. Many other codes and mechanisms are logically possible. That the same system, in its essentials, appears in bacteria, fungi, plants, and animals alike is itself strong evidence that all of life traces back to a single common ancestor that already had this system in place.

Beyond that universal starting point, the logic of molecular evidence for relationships among specific species is straightforward and testable, drawing on the genomics tools covered earlier in this course. Two species that share a more recent common ancestor have had less time, since they diverged from each other, to independently accumulate differences, or mutations, in their DNA. Two species that diverged from their common ancestor much longer ago have had more time to accumulate independent differences. So comparing DNA, or protein, sequences across species and counting how many differences have accumulated gives an estimate of how closely related those species are, and, roughly, how long ago they diverged. Humans and chimpanzees, whose lineages diverged relatively recently on an evolutionary timescale, show DNA sequences that are extremely similar, often cited as similar in the high nineties percent depending on exactly what is compared and how. Humans and more distantly related species, mice, then fish, then further out, show progressively greater sequence divergence. This lets biologists build molecular phylogenies, family trees constructed purely from sequence comparison, and a powerful confirmation of the whole approach is that these molecular trees largely agree with the family trees built independently from fossils and comparative anatomy.

One particularly striking category of molecular evidence comes from shared genetic mistakes: pseudogenes, broken, nonfunctional remnants of genes that once worked in an ancestor. Humans, along with other primates that share a relatively recent common ancestor, carry a shared, disabled version of a gene that in most other mammals still produces an enzyme needed to synthesize vitamin C internally. Because that gene is broken in these primates, they, including humans, must get vitamin C from their diet instead. The exact same gene being broken, in essentially the same way, in humans and our closest primate relatives is very difficult to explain as coincidence, two lineages independently suffering the exact same disabling mutation, but is exactly what you would expect if the mutation happened once in a shared ancestor and was simply inherited by all of its descendants. Shared errors like this are, in a sense, even more persuasive than shared functional similarities, because there is no functional reason two species would need to break the same gene in the same way unless they inherited that break from the same source.
